tool.name: RandomPointGenerator

summary.para:
View online help files: https://www.jennessent.com/geometric-tools/random-point-generator.html
Generates uniform random points inside polygon features (selection honored, holes respected), along polyline features, within the data cells of an integer raster's categories, or in a plain extent, with two optional hard constraints: a minimum separation between points, and a minimum separation from the area boundary. Very similar to Esri's Create Spatial Sampling Locations tool, with several additions (see the tool help). Stratified sampling follows the same model: strata are individual polygons or polylines, raster categories, contiguous raster regions, or groups sharing a strata ID value; counts are allocated equally, proportionally to stratum area or length, from a population field (equal or proportional), or by density (per acre, square mile, hectare or square kilometer; per foot, mile, meter or kilometer of line for polylines). An optional seed makes runs exactly reproducible. A modernized port of Jeff Jenness's classic Random Point Generator extension. Works at every license level.

tool.usage:
A modernized port of the classic Random Point Generator extension (Jenness Enterprises).
Three kinds of area of interest: • Polygons: points uniformly distributed by area; selection honored, holes respected. • Polylines: points uniformly distributed along the lines by length. • An integer raster with an attribute table: points uniformly distributed within the data cells; NoData excluded; categories come from the Value field and every output point carries its cell's Value in a Category field.
A plain extent works too. The Extent geoprocessing environment clips polygon areas when set, and for rasters it clips the read window itself -- a small analysis extent on a huge raster reads only that window, which also keeps the contiguous-region and boundary-distance options (limited to about 60 million cells in memory) available on rasters far larger than that.
The sampling design follows Esri's Create Spatial Sampling Locations stratification model. The sampling method defines the strata: • No stratification: the whole area is one stratum. • Stratify by individual polygon or polyline: each record is a stratum. • Stratify by raster category: each Value. • Stratify by contiguous raster region: each connected block of cells with the same value -- cells connected by shared edges; two same-value regions that do not touch are different strata. • Stratify by strata ID field: all polygons, polylines or raster cells sharing an integer or text ID form one stratum -- members need not be contiguous.
Stratified outputs carry a Stratum field, and feature-based strata add a Src_FID link to the source feature.
The sample count allocation method sets how many points each stratum receives: • Equal count in each stratum: give the number of samples per stratum. • Count proportional to stratum area (or length): give the overall number, distributed by exact largest-remainder apportionment. • Count equal to a population field: each stratum's own number; the field cannot be negative, and grouped strata sum their members. • Count proportional to a population field: give the field and the overall number. • By density: points per acre, square mile, hectare or square kilometer of area, or per foot, mile, meter or kilometer of line length for polylines.
Density and proportional counts come from geodesic areas and lengths (true per-row cell areas for geographic rasters), honest in any coordinate system. Unstratified sampling offers the fixed total and density.
The two separation constraints (both optional, in real units -- meters, kilometers, feet or miles): a minimum distance between points, and a minimum distance from the area boundary. Esri's Create Random Points offers only the first, evaluated in the dataset's own (possibly angular) units; this tool enforces the boundary separation exactly by insetting the area before sampling, so no buffer pre-processing step is needed. For polylines the boundary separation is measured along the line from each end (and each part's ends); for rasters it is the distance from NoData cells and the raster (or read-window) edge, resolved at cell precision.
Spatial vs along-the-line spacing (polylines only): by default the minimum distance between points is an absolute spatial distance -- no two points fall closer than that in any direction, which naturally includes distance along the line. Choosing distance measured along the polyline instead constrains only points on the same line (same part), by the distance you would travel along it -- points on separate lines never block each other, however close they pass. Why you would want this: suppose you are placing survey stations along drainage-bottom polylines and require stations at least 500 meters apart so each samples a different reach of stream. Two neighboring drainages may run parallel only 200 meters apart across a dividing ridge; with absolute spatial spacing, a station in one drainage would sterilize the adjacent reach of the neighboring drainage -- blocking perfectly good stations that are kilometers away by water. Along-the-line spacing keeps the 500-meter guarantee within each drainage while letting the neighboring drainage be sampled independently.
The third choice, network distance through connected polylines, extends this to whole stream networks: lines joined at shared endpoints or confluences (T and Y junctions, including the parts of a multipart feature) constrain each other by the distance you would travel through the network -- so a station just upstream of a fork correctly blocks the first reach of both branches, while unconnected lines still never interact. The network is built over the minimum set of lines necessary: the whole feature class when unstratified, each strata-ID group's joined segments when stratifying by ID, or a single feature's own parts when stratifying by individual polyline. Endpoints must coincide (snapped data) to count as connected; lines that merely cross without a shared endpoint -- a bridge over a stream -- do not connect.
Relation to Esri's tools. This tool is very similar to the existing Create Spatial Sampling Locations geoprocessing tool -- the stratification and allocation choices follow the same model -- except that it adds a few things: a minimum distance from the area boundary, sampling along polylines, specifying the number of points with a density value, real-unit distances that stay meaningful on geographic data, and a reproducibility seed. Two of Create Spatial Sampling Locations' output types are deliberately not duplicated here, because other Jenness Enterprises tools already produce them: its Systematic (gridded) point arrays are exactly what the Repeating Shapes tool's point patterns generate, with more arrangements and full control of spacing and orientation. Its Cluster output goes one step further -- it tessellates the study area into polygons and then keeps only a random subset of them -- and that is a two-tool recipe here: run Repeating Shapes to tessellate the study area (hexagons, squares, triangles, or rectangles), then run Select Random Records (Data Tools group) on the result to select the random subset of polygons, with the bonus that the subset can also be sized by Auto Calculate, drawn proportional to area, or made reproducible with a seed. Compared with the older Create Random Points, this tool adds the boundary distance, density counts and stratified designs. The generation is vectorized -- large point sets with tight spacings place in seconds.
When the spacing is too tight for the requested count (random packings of circles jam near 55% coverage), the tool warns up front, places as many points as fit, and reports the shortfall -- every placed point still honors the constraints. The Advanced section controls how hard it tries: the placement-attempts-per-point budget (default 1000) is how many candidate locations each requested point may consume before the tool gives up on reaching the full count. Raise it to place more points in tightly packed areas at the cost of a longer run.
Geographic data is handled in an automatic Lambert azimuthal equal-area working projection centered on the area of interest (built on the input's own datum): uniform density is exact everywhere, separation distances are true to second order at regional scales, and the output is written back in the input geographic coordinate system.
The random seed makes runs exactly reproducible: the same inputs with the same seed give the same points. Leave it blank for a fresh draw each run.
Output: a point feature class with a Point_ID field; stratified runs add a Stratum field, feature-based strata add Src_FID, and raster runs add the cell's Category. The output inherits the boundary's coordinate system unless the Output Coordinate System environment says otherwise.

param.name: boundary
param.displayname: Area of interest (polygons, polylines, or an integer raster with an attribute table; optional -- else the extent below)

dialogReference.para: The area of interest: polygons to fill (holes and multipart shapes handled), polylines to place points along, or an integer raster with an attribute table (NoData excluded; categories from the Value field). Selections are honored. Leave blank to use the extent parameter instead.

param.name: extent
param.displayname: Extent (used when no area of interest is given; the Extent environment clips polygon areas)

dialogReference.para: A plain rectangular area, used when no area of interest is given. The Extent geoprocessing environment clips polygon areas when set.

param.name: strata_method
param.displayname: Sampling method (how the strata are defined)

bulletList.bullet_item: None: the whole area is one stratum.
Each individual polygon or polyline is a stratum.
Each contiguous raster region: cells of one value connected by shared edges; disconnected same-value regions are different strata.
Groups sharing a strata ID value.

dialogReference.para: The choices are phrased to match the input.

param.name: strata_field
param.displayname: Strata ID field (integer or text; polygons, polylines, or a raster attribute-table field)

dialogReference.para: The integer or text field whose values group polygons, polylines or raster categories into strata (members need not be contiguous). The ObjectID field also qualifies (equivalent to stratifying by individual feature). For rasters this is a field of the attribute table.

How many points each stratum receives: an equal count, a count proportional to stratum area (or length), a count equal to or proportional to a population field, or a density. Unstratified sampling offers the fixed total and density.

param.name: n_points
param.displayname: Number of samples (the total, spread across the strata)

dialogReference.para: The overall number of samples, distributed across the strata (proportional methods) or the whole area in proportion to area or length.
The number of samples each stratum receives (equal-count allocation).

param.name: population_field
param.displayname: Population field (non-negative; per feature, or a raster attribute-table field)

dialogReference.para: A non-negative numeric field driving the equal-to or proportional-to population allocations: per polygon or polyline (a grouped stratum sums its members), or a raster attribute-table field per category.

param.name: density
param.displayname: Density: points per unit (area unit; length unit for polylines)

dialogReference.para: How many points per unit, e.g. 0.5 points per hectare -- or per mile of line for polylines, or per hectare of each category for rasters. Counts come from geodesic areas and lengths, honest in any coordinate system.
The unit the density refers to: Acre, Square Mile, Hectare or Square Kilometer for areas; Foot, Mile, Meter or Kilometer of line length for polylines.
No two points will fall closer together than this (a hard constraint). If the count cannot be met at this spacing the tool warns and places as many as fit.

param.name: spacing_type
param.displayname: How the minimum distance is measured (polylines only)

dialogReference.para: Polylines only: how the minimum distance is measured.

bulletList.bullet_item: Absolute spatial distance (the default): no two points closer than this in any direction.

Along the polyline: only points on the same line constrain each other, so separate lines never block one another -- e.g. stations 500 m apart along drainage bottoms without blocking the parallel drainage 200 m over the ridge.

Network distance through connected lines: travel distance through shared endpoints and confluences, so a station near a fork guards both branches; built per strata group, and joins a multipart feature's own parts.

param.name: boundary_gap
param.displayname: Minimum distance from the area boundary (optional; polylines: from each end along the line; rasters: from NoData/edge cells)

dialogReference.para: No point will fall closer to the area's boundary than this -- polygon outer edges and hole edges; for polylines, measured along the line from each end; for rasters, the distance from NoData/edge cells. The constraint Esri's Create Random Points lacks.

param.name: linear_units
param.displayname: Units for the two distances above

dialogReference.para: Units for the two distances above: Meters, Kilometers, Feet or Miles.

param.name: random_seed
param.displayname: Random seed (optional -- same seed, same points)

dialogReference.para: Optional: the same seed with the same inputs reproduces the same points exactly. Leave blank for a fresh draw each run.

param.name: max_attempts
param.displayname: Placement attempts per point before giving up (used when a minimum spacing is set)

dialogReference.para: Advanced: how many candidate placements each point may consume before the tool gives up on reaching the full count (used when a minimum spacing is set; default 1000). Raise it to push harder toward the requested count in tightly packed areas -- the run takes longer but places more points; lower it for faster give-up.
The output point feature class, with Point_ID; stratified runs add a Stratum field, feature-based strata add Src_FID, and raster runs add the cell's Category.

scriptExample.title: Random Point Generator example (stand-alone script)
scriptExample.para: Half a point per hectare, at least 100 m apart and 50 m inside the boundary, reproducible with a seed.
scriptExample.code: import arcpy arcpy.ImportToolbox(r"C:\path\to\JennessEnterprisesTools.pyt") # your install path # strata_method options (matching is by prefix): # "No stratification (the whole area is one stratum)" # "Stratify by individual polygon" / "... polyline" # "Stratify by raster category (Value field)" # "Stratify by contiguous raster region" # "Stratify by strata ID field" (+ strata_field) # alloc_method options: # "Fixed total number of points" (unstratified) # "Equal count in each stratum" (+ n_per_stratum) # "Count proportional to stratum area" (+ n_points) # "Count equal to a population field" (+ population_field) # "Count proportional to a population field" # "By density (points per area unit)" / "... length unit" # density_units: "Acre" / "Square Mile" / "Hectare" / "Square Kilometer" # (for polylines: "Foot" / "Mile" / "Meter" / "Kilometer") # linear_units: "Meters" / "Kilometers" / "Feet" / "Miles" arcpy.jenness.RandomPointGenerator( boundary=r"D:\data\study.gdb\subplots", strata_method="Stratify by individual polygon", alloc_method="By density (points per area unit)", density=0.5, density_units="Hectare", min_spacing=100.0, boundary_gap=50.0, linear_units="Meters", random_seed=42, out_fc=r"D:\data\study.gdb\sample_points")
